prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Houston, Texas, had a record high temperature Wednesday as a heat wave continues to grip the nation's midsection, the National Weather Service said Thursday. A woman tries to beat Houston's record heat by lying on a bench in the shade. The city sweltered with a high temperature of 104 degrees Wednesday, a record high for June 24, forecasters said. The previous record high for the date was 99 degrees, set in 1980. The previous record high measured for the month of June in Houston was 103 degrees, set on June 30, 1980, and June 18, 1934. Heat indices, a combination of temperature and humidity, are breaking the 110-degree mark in many cities. Forecasters predicted a high near 100 for Houston on Thursday, but the temperature could rise into the triple digits in outlying areas, said CNN meteorologist Reynolds Wolf. The weather service posted heat advisories for Houston; Dallas, Texas; and New Orleans, Louisiana, indicating that temperatures in those cities will feel like 100 to 105 degrees because of high humidity. In the Houston community of Bayland Park, the elderly were taking advantage of the air-conditioned Community Center. "I don't like hot weather. I never have and never will," Teet Charloton told CNN affiliate KPRC-TV in Houston. "But we have to have it. I go from the car to the house or come in here and go back the same way. I don't do much shopping, that's for sure." Betty Dante added, "It is very hot outside. ... I think as you get older, you feel the heat more." In southwest Houston, Leticia Alvarado is profiting from the heat. The unemployed Houstonian has been running along the median on Hillcroft Street at Bellaire Boulevard for seven weeks. She is selling water for $1 a bottle. "It's hot, too hot," she told the station. Other cities also were sweltering. New Iberia, Louisiana, had a temperature Wednesday of 102, which broke the record of 97 in 2005. An excessive heat warning was issued for St. Louis, Missouri, on Thursday through 7 p.m. CT Saturday. Forecasters predicted a high near 96. Cloud cover was expected to make temperatures there a little cooler Thursday, but the weather service warned, "A hot and humid air mass remains over the area which will continue to control weather over the region through Saturday." Afternoon and early evening heat index readings of 100 to 110 were expected in the Missouri city every day through Saturday. Young children, the elderly and people with chronic sicknesses were advised to stay inside if possible. The heat wave that began last week was being fed by a high pressure system north of Texas . Air quality alerts were posted for several cities, indicating pollutants exceed accepted standards. A red alert was issued for Houston, the third most severe alert that indicates unhealthy air quality.

Houston’s temperature reached 104 degrees Wednesday, the hottest ever recorded in the city on June 24. The previous record for that date was 99 degrees, established in 1980. Wednesday’s reading also surpassed Houston’s earlier June record of 103 degrees, recorded on both June 30, 1980, and June 18, 1934.

In many cities, heat-index values—which account for both temperature and humidity—were exceeding 110 degrees. Houston was expected to approach 100 degrees Thursday, while surrounding areas could climb above the century mark, according to CNN meteorologist Reynolds Wolf.

Teet Charloton told CNN affiliate KPRC-TV that she had always disliked hot weather. She said she limited her movements to traveling between her car, home and the center, and largely avoided shopping. Betty Dante said the outdoor heat was intense and suggested that people become more sensitive to it as they age.

Elsewhere in southwest Houston, Leticia Alvarado was earning money because of the high temperatures. The unemployed Houston resident had spent seven weeks running along the median of Hillcroft Street at Bellaire Boulevard, selling bottled water for $1 each. She described the weather to the station as excessively hot.

Other communities were also enduring record heat. New Iberia, Louisiana, reached 102 degrees Wednesday, surpassing the previous record of 97 set in 2005.

In St. Louis, Missouri, an excessive heat warning took effect Thursday and was scheduled to remain in place until 7 p.m. Central Time Saturday. Forecasters expected the temperature to peak near 96 degrees. Although clouds were likely to make Thursday slightly cooler, the weather service said a hot, humid air mass would continue to dominate the region’s weather through Saturday.

St. Louis was forecast to experience heat-index readings between 100 and 110 degrees during the afternoon and early evening each day through Saturday. Officials advised young children, older adults and people with chronic illnesses to remain indoors whenever possible.

The heat wave, which began the previous week, was being sustained by a high-pressure system located north of Texas. Air-quality alerts were also issued in several cities because pollution levels exceeded accepted limits. Houston was placed under a red alert, the third-highest severity level, signifying unhealthy air quality.

# Houston hits record 104 degrees as heat wave grips central United States

**Houston** — Houston reached a record high of 104 degrees on June 24 as a dangerous heat wave continued to bake parts of the central United States.

The temperature surpassed the city’s previous record for the date, adding to a stretch of unusually intense early-summer heat across Texas and neighboring states. High humidity made conditions feel even hotter, increasing the risk of heat-related illness for people spending extended periods outdoors.

Excessive heat alerts were in effect across parts of the region as forecasters warned that overnight temperatures would provide little relief. Warm nights can heighten health risks because the body has less time to recover from daytime heat.

Officials urged residents to drink plenty of water, limit strenuous outdoor activity during the hottest part of the day and check on older adults, young children and people without reliable air conditioning. Health experts also warned never to leave children or pets in parked vehicles, where temperatures can become deadly within minutes.

The heat also placed added strain on power systems as air-conditioning demand climbed. Outdoor workers and people experiencing homelessness were among those facing the greatest exposure.

Meteorologists said a persistent area of high pressure helped trap hot air over the central United States, producing widespread temperatures near or above 100 degrees. Such patterns, often described as heat domes, can linger for days and suppress cooling clouds and rain.

Although individual heat waves are influenced by short-term weather patterns, scientists say human-caused climate change is making extreme heat events more frequent and intense.

Forecasters advised residents to continue monitoring local warnings, with dangerous heat expected to remain a concern across portions of the central US.

A persistent heat dome brought dangerous temperatures from Texas to the lower Mississippi Valley and Midwest, prompting excessive-heat warnings, energy-conservation appeals and air-quality alerts.

- **Houston:** Bush Intercontinental Airport reached **109°F**, tying Houston’s all-time official high. The National Weather Service issued excessive-heat warnings as heat-index values climbed well above 110°F. Ozone-action alerts were also posted because sunlight, stagnant air and vehicle emissions produced unhealthy pollution levels, especially for children, older adults and people with respiratory conditions.

- **Dallas–Fort Worth:** Temperatures rose to approximately **109–110°F**, setting or tying daily records, although remaining below the area’s all-time record of 113°F. Authorities warned that repeated triple-digit days and warm nights increased the risk of heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Air-quality alerts focused mainly on elevated ground-level ozone.

- **New Orleans:** Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport recorded **105°F on Aug. 27**, establishing a new all-time temperature record for the city’s official observing site. High humidity pushed “feels-like” readings substantially higher. Excessive-heat warnings remained in effect, while air-quality advisories cautioned residents with asthma and other lung conditions to limit strenuous outdoor activity.

- **St. Louis:** Temperatures climbed into the low 100s, with heat-index readings around **115°F or higher** in parts of the region. Excessive-heat warnings covered the metropolitan area. Local agencies also issued ozone-related air-quality alerts as stagnant conditions trapped pollutants near the surface.

Residents across the four cities described the heat as oppressive and unusually persistent. People reported changing work and exercise schedules, staying indoors during the afternoon, carrying extra water and relying heavily on air conditioning. Outdoor workers and people without reliable cooling expressed particular concern, while some residents said even early mornings and evenings offered little relief.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed news story explaining how a high-pressure system north of Texas is causing dangerous heat indices across the nation’s midsection.
counterfactuals.output:
# High-pressure system fuels dangerous heat across nation’s midsection

**A sprawling dome of high pressure centered north of Texas is trapping hot, humid air over the central United States, producing dangerous heat indices from the southern Plains into the Midwest.**

The weather pattern is bringing more than simply high afternoon temperatures. Moisture flowing north from the Gulf of Mexico is combining with sinking air beneath the high-pressure system, making conditions feel significantly hotter than thermometer readings suggest. In some communities, the apparent temperature could reach or exceed 105 degrees during the hottest part of the day.

High-pressure systems naturally suppress clouds and thunderstorms by forcing air downward. As that air sinks, it compresses and warms. Clearer skies also allow intense summer sunlight to heat the ground for longer periods, while light winds near the center of the system provide little relief.

When a strong high remains in place for several days, the effect is often described as a “heat dome.” The atmosphere acts like a lid, limiting the ability of hot air near the surface to rise and disperse. Soils can dry out, vegetation loses moisture and each successive day may begin warmer than the last.

The location of the high north of Texas is especially important. Clockwise circulation around the system is helping draw warm, moisture-laden air out of the Gulf and into parts of the Plains, Mississippi Valley and Midwest. That humidity slows the evaporation of sweat, the body’s primary cooling mechanism.

The result is a dangerous increase in the heat index — a measure of how hot conditions feel when air temperature and relative humidity are considered together. An air temperature in the upper 90s, for example, can feel well above 105 degrees when humidity is high.

The risk does not end at sunset. Humid air cools slowly, and overnight temperatures in many cities may remain in the upper 70s or warmer. Those elevated nighttime readings can place additional strain on the body because people without reliable air conditioning receive little opportunity to recover.

Urban areas are particularly vulnerable. Asphalt, concrete and rooftops absorb heat during the day and release it after dark, creating an urban heat-island effect. Temperatures can remain several degrees warmer in densely developed neighborhoods than in surrounding rural areas.

Agricultural regions may also contribute additional near-surface humidity. Crops such as corn release water vapor through a process called transpiration, sometimes informally called “corn sweat.” Across large areas of mature crops, that moisture can push dew points higher and worsen heat-index values.

Health officials warn that prolonged exposure can lead to heat exhaustion or heat stroke. Symptoms of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, weakness and headache. Heat stroke is a medical emergency and may involve confusion, loss of consciousness, hot skin or a body temperature of 103 degrees or higher.

Older adults, young children, outdoor workers, athletes and people with chronic health conditions face heightened danger. Those without air conditioning, including residents of older homes and people experiencing homelessness, are also at greater risk.

Emergency managers recommend limiting strenuous outdoor activity during the afternoon, drinking water regularly and taking frequent breaks in air-conditioned spaces. Alcohol and excessive caffeine can contribute to dehydration. Officials also urge residents to check on neighbors and relatives and never leave children or pets inside parked vehicles, where temperatures can rise to deadly levels within minutes.

The heat is also expected to increase electricity demand as homes and businesses rely heavily on air conditioning. Utilities typically monitor the power grid closely during extended hot spells because demand can remain high into the evening, particularly when overnight temperatures offer little relief.

Relief will depend on when the high-pressure ridge weakens or shifts. A passing cold front could eventually bring thunderstorms and somewhat cooler air to the northern edge of the heat dome, but areas closer to the center may remain hot for longer. Storms developing along the boundary could also become severe, fueled by the same heat and moisture building across the region.

Until the pattern changes, forecasters say the combination of intense sunshine, Gulf humidity and unusually warm nights will keep heat-related illness a serious concern across much of the nation’s midsection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
